scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Arjuna Nritham, also called Mayilpeeli Thookkam, is rooted in the Bhagavathy temple traditions of south Kerala.
The dance refers to the Mahabharatha legend in which Arjuna propitiates goddess Bhadrakali through a devotional performance.
The art form has been preserved and transmitted through generations by men of the Ezhava community, as well as the Ashari and Kollan communities, predominantly in Kottayam and Alappuzha districts.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed as an all-night devotional ritual to propitiate goddess Bhadrakali.
The costume and facial cosmetics are designed to evoke the hero Arjuna performing his act of devotion.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance movements are known as Pyattu and draw directly from the martial techniques of Kalarippayattu.
Executed solo or in pairs during all-night performances, the dance is strictly tied to rhythmic songs called Kavithangal.
Dancers verbally explain the specific rhythmic structure of each song to the gathered audience before physically translating those drum patterns into stepping and stance sequences.
Watch for Pyattu.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music for Arjuna Nritham centers on Kavithangal, rhythm-driven vocal compositions detailing stories from the Hindu Puranas.
Musical accompaniment is provided by percussion instruments characteristic of Kerala temple arts, specifically the chenda, talachenda, and ilathalam (cymbals).
Listen for the chenda, talachenda, ilathalam.
The pulse is Varies according to specific Kavitham rhythm compositions explained by the dancer.
Resonant heavy percussion driven by chenda and talachenda drums punctuated by metallic ilathalam cymbals, accompanied by vocal recital of puranic stories.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performances occur in Bhagavathy temples.

Dancers wear green facial makeup, ornate headgear known as Nettipattom, and a distinctive lower body garment crafted from peacock feathers (mayilppeeli) fastened around the waist in the manner of Kathakali's uduthukettu.
